extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of journalism, political science, sociology, and readers interested in how public opinion and stereotypes form
extracted.subtask_description: The page offers theoretical criteria for understanding how media, stereotypes, experts, and social codes shape public opinion and perception. It identifies mechanisms (images, reinforcement, defenses, blind spots) and practical consequences for political behavior and propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of photographs and moving pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs have the kind of authority over imagination to-day, which the printed word had yesterday, and the spoken word before that. They seem utterly real.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moving pictures and photographs appear to come directly to us 'without human meddling' and supply effortless, vivid images that replace the need to imagine; a single filmic depiction can fix an association (e.g., Birth of a Nation shaping the Ku Klux Klan image) and persist even if historically or morally wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish instinctive equipment from stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: When we speak of the mind of a group we must 'separate the instinctive equipment from the stereotypes, the patterns, and the formulae' that build the mental world people respond to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attributing political or cultural differences to biological or innate factors; instead, examine transmitted institutions (nursery, school, church, family) as primary sources of political habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political habits are learned, not biological
rubrics_metrics.description: There is not the least scientific evidence that men are born with the political habits of the country in which they are born.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To explain shared political habits in a nation, first look to upbringing and social institutions rather than to 'Group Minds' or 'National Souls'; resist biologizing cultural differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes as defenses of social position
rubrics_metrics.description: The systems of stereotypes may be the core of our personal tradition, the defenses of our position in society. They are an ordered picture of a possible world to which our habits and hopes have adjusted themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that stereotypes preserve self-respect and social order; challenges to a stereotype are experienced as personal or existential attacks, so rhetoric that threatens stereotypes will be resisted even when inaccurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes precede reasoning and shape perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfect stereotype 'precedes the use of reason; is a form of perception, imposes a certain character on the data of our senses before the data reach the intelligence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that stereotypes filter and 'stamp' incoming evidence, so investigation should attempt to identify and bracket preconceptions; accounts (e.g., travelers) often tell us more about what the observer carried with him than about the observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinforcement vs. dismissal of contradictory evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If what we are looking at corresponds with what we anticipated, the stereotype is reinforced; if the experience contradicts the stereotype, either it is dismissed as an exception or it modifies the stereotype depending on plasticity and interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether observers reinterpret, discredit, or assimilate exceptions; measure openness to revision as a key factor in whether public belief changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes are affectively charged
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes are highly charged with the feelings that are attached to them. They are the fortress of our tradition, and behind its defenses we can continue to feel ourselves safe in the position we occupy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for emotional investment when analyzing public adherence to beliefs—logical refutation alone may not dislodge a stereotype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes can be constructed to justify institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: Aristotle's defense of slavery is a stereotype that 'teaches the Greeks a way of seeing their slaves that comported with the continuance of slavery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize rhetorical techniques that frame social relations as 'natural' to exclude doubt; watch for circular reasoning where the fact (e.g., people are slaves) is used to prove the naturalness of that fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legends and atrocity tales exploit gaps and ambiguities
rubrics_metrics.description: Where so much is left to the imagination—e.g., the fog of war—there is no check and no control, so legends (atrocity stories) spread and tap old hatreds and associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In information-sparse environments, expect false or exaggerated narratives to fill gaps; propagandists and censors may deliberately disseminate such legends because of their mobilizing power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes economize attention but create blind spots
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes save time and focus energy, but they also censor out much that needs to be taken into account; when shattered they can 'ship-wreck' considerations that had been taken into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both the functional benefits (rapid action, mobilization) and the costs (ignored complexity, poor adaptation in changing circumstances); look for moments when blind spots move from margin to center (e.g., postwar planning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Models and idealized theories differ from popularized current versions
rubrics_metrics.description: What operates in history is not the systematic idea as a genius formulated it, but shifting imitations, replicas, counterfeits, analogies, and distortions in individual minds (e.g., 'Das Kapital' as conceived vs. Das Kapital as understood).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing political movements or doctrines, study how ideas are actually preached, interpreted, and administered among the public rather than relying solely on canonical texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise multiplies perceivable aspects and may intensify stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Expertness is a multiplication of the number of aspects we are prepared to discover, plus the habit of discounting our expectations; but a little expertness may simply exaggerate the habit of fitting facts into stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish genuine broadened perception from narrow professional tunnel-vision; trained observers should still guard against overfitting facts to existing frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas penetrate public consciousness when tied to concrete evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: An idea must have external and concrete embodiment, or be recommended by striking material evidence, to penetrate general consciousness (example: mechanical revolution made 'progress' believable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the material or sensory supports that allow abstract ideas to generalize; policy messaging that links abstract claims to visible evidence will spread more readily.

rubrics_metrics.name: American stereotype of progress privileges quantitative and mechanical criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: In America the spectacle of mechanical progress has suffused the moral code: excellence is confused with size, happiness with speed, and human nature with contraption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing American public opinion, note tendencies to equate 'bigger/faster' with 'better' and to overlook negative by-products (e.g., slums, unassimilated immigration, depletion of resources).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes influence aims and limit reflection in mobilization
rubrics_metrics.description: The progressive stereotype 'almost completely obliterates the attempt to decide what work and why that work'—it focuses on means (scale, speed) and neglects ends (what is the purpose of victory or production?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate campaigns and mobilizations for whether they adopt instrumental stereotypes that obscure or omit deliberation about ultimate objectives; policy should interrogate ends as well as means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplified economic models can become pervasive mythologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Economists' simplified diagrams (capitalist, entrepreneur, freely contracting workers, consumers maximizing pleasure) were popularized until for large sections they prevailed as the economic mythology of the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of stylized models turned into prescriptive worldviews; empirical inquiry should test whether the model's assumed actors and incentives actually obtain in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Studying actual public culture requires finding unbiassed trained observers
rubrics_metrics.description: The actual culture exists in people 'far too busy to indulge in the strange trade of formulating their beliefs.' The best we can do is follow suggestions to 'move freely among all sorts and conditions of men' and seek unbiassed persons with skill in sizing up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In empirical studies of opinion, prioritize methodological diversity, field observation, and seeking informants who are less invested in rhetorical formulations; accept the large element of guesswork and the difficulty of knowing typicality.
